Terrestrial
te-RES-tree-al
adjective
From the Latin terrestris, belonging to the earth, from terra, the earth. Of or pertaining to the earth, as celestial is of the heavens; the two words are set in deliberate contrast by Paul.

Biblical Definition

The word belongs to Paul’s great argument on the resurrection body: “There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another” (1Co 15:40). He is answering the scoffing question with what body do they come? and his method is to multiply examples of God’s power to give differing bodies. There is more than one kind of flesh; there are bodies of earth and bodies of sky; and even within the sky, “there is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory” (1Co 15:41). The point is not that the resurrection body is a star but that God’s repertoire of bodies is vast, and the objector’s failure of imagination is no argument. Then comes the conclusion: “It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1Co 15:44). Note that spiritual there does not mean immaterial — the risen Christ ate broiled fish and invited Thomas to handle Him. It means a body animated and governed by the Spirit rather than by the mere soul-life of Adam. The Christian hope is not escape from a body but the raising of one, and the terrestrial is not despised. It is sown.

Webster 1828 Definition

Belonging to the earth; earthly, as distinguished from celestial, belonging to the heavens. Used by Paul in his argument for the resurrection body.

TERRESTRIAL, adj. Pertaining to the earth; existing on the earth; earthly.

From the Latin terrestris, from terra, the earth.

Consisting of earth; as, terrestrial matter.

Opposed to celestial, which pertains to the heavens.

1Co 15:40 sets the two in contrast to illustrate differing glories of bodies.

Key Scripture

1Co 15:40 — "There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another."

1Co 15:41 — "There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory."

1Co 15:44 — "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body."

1Co 15:53 — "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality."

Modern Corruption

The Christian hope is popularly imagined as disembodied souls in a spiritual realm — a Greek idea, not a biblical one — where Paul’s whole argument is for a body raised.

expand to see more

The corruption is Platonism wearing Christian clothes. The picture most people carry — including a great many believers — is of the soul escaping the body at death and existing thereafter in a bodiless spiritual state, with matter left behind as the discarded husk of a lower existence. That is Greek philosophy, not Scripture. The Bible’s hope is resurrection: the same person raised, embodied, glorified. The confusion is helped along by the word spiritual in 1Co 15:44, which readers take to mean non-physical. Paul means a body enlivened and ruled by the Spirit, in contrast to the natural or soulish body of the first Adam. He is contrasting two animating principles, not matter with non-matter.

Recover the plain sense: the risen Christ is the specimen, and He was unmistakably physical — He showed His hands and His feet, said a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have, ate before them, and bore the marks. He is the firstfruits, which means His body is the pattern of ours. And note what this implies for the present: the body is not a temporary container for the real self but part of what is redeemed, which is why Scripture legislates for it, why fornication is a sin against one’s own body, and why burial rather than disposal has been the Christian instinct. This corruptible must put on incorruption (1Co 15:53) — this one. Not a replacement, and not an escape.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin terra, the earth — earthly, set against celestial; Paul’s illustration of the many glories God can give a body.

expand to see more

Terrestrial — Latin terrestris, from terra, the earth.

Set in deliberate contrast with celestial, of the heavens.

1Co 15:40–41 multiplies examples: earth, sky, sun, moon, star differing from star.

1Co 15:44: spiritual body means Spirit-animated, not immaterial.

1Co 15:53: this corruptible must put on incorruption.

Usage

"Paul’s answer to with what body do they come? is the variety of bodies God already makes."

"Spiritual contrasts animating principles, not matter with non-matter."

"The risen Christ ate and was handled — He is the pattern of the raised body."
